analysis.one_liner: Caps seniors' Medicare drug costs at $2,000 a year and requires drug makers to give discounts.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: introduced April 2022 with no cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cap what Medicare beneficiaries pay out of pocket for prescription drugs at $2,000 a year starting in 2025, eliminating the coverage gap (the 'donut hole') where seniors previously owed thousands more. To pay for the richer coverage, it would require brand-name drug makers to give Medicare enrollees a 10% discount off the negotiated price of their drugs below the cap, and 20% off above it. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare enrollees who take expensive prescription drugs. Today their out-of-pocket costs can run into the thousands once they hit the coverage gap; under the bill, no one in the drug benefit would owe more than $2,000 a year, and the cap would rise only with inflation in later years.

how_it_helps.text: Sets the annual out-of-pocket threshold for Medicare's drug benefit at $2,000 for 2025, with later years' caps increased by an annual inflation adjustment.
Eliminates the Part D coverage-gap cost-sharing structure for 2025 and beyond, ending the period in which beneficiaries owed a larger share of their drug costs.

Creates a manufacturer discount program requiring brand-name drug makers to provide discounted prices on their drugs dispensed to Medicare beneficiaries above the deductible: 90% of the negotiated price below the out-of-pocket cap, and 80% above it.

Requires pharmacies and mail-order services to be reimbursed the difference between the negotiated and discounted price within 14 days (electronic claims) or 30 days, so the discount reaches beneficiaries at the counter.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who must hand over mandatory discounts on every applicable drug dispensed to Medicare enrollees. Part D insurers also absorb a larger share of costs above the $2,000 cap, since the federal reinsurance rate drops from 80% to 20-40% depending on the drug.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: Beneficiaries are not fully protected below the cap: they still owe the annual deductible, coinsurance, and dispensing fees before reaching $2,000 in out-of-pocket spending.
The cap and discounts apply only to drugs covered under the Part D benefit; drug costs outside that benefit are not capped.

A manufacturer may terminate its discount agreement for any reason; the termination does not take effect until after the plan year, but the mechanism gives drug makers an exit if they choose not to participate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors on expensive drug regimens the benefit is large and concrete: a hard $2,000 ceiling on a bill that can otherwise run to many thousands in a bad year. The cost falls mainly on brand-name drug makers, whose argument that mandatory discounts discourage research on new drugs is a real but contested objection. The design is narrower than a universal fix — it covers only the Medicare drug benefit and leaves beneficiaries paying deductibles and coinsurance up to the cap — but the core trade-off strongly favors patients over manufacturers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Raphael Warnock introduced the bill on April 6, 2022; it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever taken: the bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers initially avoided this bill's mandatory discounts. The reprieve was short-lived, however: Congress enacted a nearly identical package — a $2,000 out-of-pocket cap and a mandatory manufacturer discount program for Medicare drugs — in the Inflation Reduction Act a few months later, so seniors ultimately got much of what this bill promised through a different vehicle.

for.name: Sen. Raphael Warnock
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration after its referral; it received no markup, hearing action, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so its support never took a measurable partisan shape in the record.

industries.note: The bill imposes a mandatory discount program — 10% off the negotiated price for Medicare enrollees below the $2,000 cap, 20% above it — directly cutting manufacturer revenue on drugs dispensed to seniors. The industry's cost is the public's saving.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and prescription drug plans
industries.note: Plans take on more liability above the $2,000 cap as federal reinsurance drops from 80% to 20-40% of costs, but manufacturer discounts offset part of that, and their role as the exclusive delivery channel for the Medicare drug benefit is left intact.
